data.title: Chart
data.tagline: A chart is a way to compare and understand data through visual encodings such as position, length, size, or color.
data.learningOutcome: You can choose a chart for a comparison question and check that its title, axes, legend, values, and alternative explanation make the result understandable.
data.description: A line chart can show orders changing by month, while a bar chart compares counts across channels. Charts make trends and differences easier to notice. They are not the data itself and do not replace a precise table people must check item by item or prove causation.

learning.assumes: You have seen a bar chart, line chart, or dashboard.
learning.outcome: You can choose a chart for a comparison question and check that its title, axes, legend, values, and alternative explanation make the result understandable.

distinctions.label: Table
distinctions.explanation: A Chart uses position, length, or color to reveal trends and differences. A Table preserves exact fields in rows and columns for record-by-record comparison.

explanation.title: Encoding should fit the comparison
explanation.text: Bar charts commonly compare category sizes; line charts commonly show change over time. Ask what people need to compare before choosing a visually exciting shape.

explanation.title: Reading a chart needs context
explanation.text: Title, time range, unit, axes, and legend tell people what data says. Provide labels, tooltips, or a table for important exact values; color cannot be the only cue.

data.boundary: A chart is not the whole report and cannot automatically explain why something happened. It visualizes data relationships but still needs a source, time range, and necessary explanation. A table is often better for checking each amount or exporting.

lessonPractice.title: Operations wants to compare this month's order counts from four channels. Which display fits best?

options.label: Use a bar chart with clear channel names, units, and values to compare the four channels, adding a data table when needed
options.feedback: Correct. Bar length makes category counts easy to compare, while labels and values keep the result checkable.

options.label: Use only a colorful ring with no legend or values and rely on color to feel the difference
options.feedback: People cannot reliably tell what each color means or the precise difference.

options.label: Draw a trend line then state that ads caused orders to grow without other evidence
options.feedback: A chart can show changes happening together; it cannot prove causation on its own.

data.agentPrompt: Turn this month's order counts from four channels into a bar chart with a clear title, month, unit, channel names, and a value for each bar; do not rely on color alone. Verify that keyboard or screen-reader users can get the same key information and retain a checkable data table.
